---
title: "A Short History of Atomic Layer Deposition"
---

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
## Learning outcomes
After this chapter you should be able to:

1. Describe the two independent origins of ALD: molecular layering in the Soviet Union and atomic layer epitaxy in Finland.
2. Explain why the technique's first industrial use was in displays, and what moved it into semiconductor manufacturing.
3. Explain why some of the field's terminology ("epitaxy", "atomic layer") is historically rooted rather than physically accurate.
:::

## Two inventions, one technique

ALD was discovered independently at least twice, under different names [@Ahvenniemi2017; @Puurunen2014; @Barry2022]:

- **Molecular layering (ML)**, developed in Leningrad from the 1960s by V. B. Aleskovskii and his student S. I. Kol'tsov [@Malygin2015; @Barry2022].
- **Atomic layer epitaxy (ALE)**, developed in Finland from 1974 by Tuomo Suntola and co-workers [@Puurunen2014].

Both rest on the principle from @sec-what-makes-ald: repeated, separate, saturating gas–solid reactions. They reached it from opposite directions, though, and each lineage left its mark on how ALD is thought about today.

### Molecular layering: a chemical question

The Leningrad work started from a question about solids, not films. In his 1952 doctoral thesis at the Leningrad Technological Institute, Aleskovskii proposed what he called the "matrix" or "framework" hypothesis [@Malygin2015; @Barry2022]. A solid framework carries a stoichiometric number of reactive surface sites relative to its bulk atoms. If those sites are reacted with a suitable chemical, the result is a new surface that again carries a stoichiometric number of sites. The cyclical logic of ALD is already present in this idea: each reaction regenerates the conditions for the next [@Barry2022].

The method followed over the next two decades [@Barry2022]:

- **1963:** first report of molecular layering, in the Russian literature.
- **1965:** first full paper, by Aleskovskii in *J. Appl. Chem. USSR*.
- **1971:** Kol'tsov's doctoral dissertation, which contains much of what would now be called the chemical conceptualization of ALD. In the same year, Kol'tsov and Aleskovskii applied for a patent titled "The Principles of Synthesis of Solids". It was declined.

Throughout, molecular layering was framed as surface chemistry: how to change a material's surface by chemical means, producing different kinds of surfaces and different ratios of bulk atoms to surface sites [@Barry2022]. Because it was published mainly in Russian, it reached few readers outside the USSR. A detailed English-language account of Aleskovskii and Kol'tsov's work only appeared in 2015 [@Malygin2015].

### Atomic layer epitaxy: an engineering answer

In 1974, the Finnish medical-technology company Instrumentarium asked Suntola, a young physicist, to lead a new R&D effort. He chose thin-film electroluminescent (EL) displays. These need very thin, uniform, pinhole-free films with high dielectric strength, over large areas. The original target was high-quality **polycrystalline ZnS** for EL panels [@Puurunen2014].

Suntola and Jorma Antson filed the patent "Method for Producing Compound Thin Films" in 1974 [@Puurunen2014; @Barry2022]. Where molecular layering asked a chemical question, ALE was engineered from the start as an industrial solution for making devices, and it focused on the physics and engineering of depositing and characterizing films [@Barry2022]. The patent shows this. It contains detailed technical drawings of a reactor, and the ALE work laid the technical foundations of concepts that are now active research areas in their own right, including area-selective ALD and spatial ALD [@Barry2022].

In 1977 the team moved to Lohja Corporation, which built an electronics factory in Espoo in 1984 to make ALE-grown ZnS:Mn displays. This was the first industrial use of the technique. Display modules from the line served in the departure hall of Helsinki-Vantaa airport for about two decades. Suntola's display work also explains why early ALD concentrated on chalcogenides (sulfides and selenides); oxides and nitrides came to the fore in the 1990s [@Barry2022].

### A missed connection

The two lineages developed without collaboration, and very likely without knowledge of each other. Given how differently they were framed, that is not surprising: one was about the chemistry of a surface relative to the bulk, the other about the engineering of thin-film devices [@Barry2022].

They did come close to meeting. In the late 1970s, Suntola defended his patent application in Moscow, and the patent was granted in the Soviet jurisdiction. The examiners did not raise molecular layering as prior art, and an early chance to join the two bodies of work was missed [@Barry2022]. The connection was eventually made decades later, largely through the historical work of Riikka Puurunen and the VPHA (see below) [@Barry2022; @Ahvenniemi2017].

| | Molecular layering | Atomic layer epitaxy |
|---|---|---|
| Where | Leningrad Technological Institute, USSR | Instrumentarium, then Lohja, Finland |
| Key people | V. B. Aleskovskii, S. I. Kol'tsov | T. Suntola, J. Antson |
| Origin | 1952 "framework" hypothesis; first reports 1963–1965 | 1974 patent application |
| Framing | Chemistry: modifying the surface of a solid | Engineering: depositing films for devices |
| Patent | 1971 application declined | Granted, including in the USSR |
| Reach | Published mainly in Russian | International patents and conferences |

: The two origins of ALD compared [@Malygin2015; @Puurunen2014; @Barry2022]. {#tbl-origins}

The way we draw ALD has changed with the field. Kol'tsov's 1971 thesis pictured the growing surface as a regular lattice of atomic points, one layer added per cycle. Modern depictions, such as Puurunen's, show bulky chemisorbed precursor fragments and the complexity of the surface reactions [@Barry2022]. Simulation 2.1 in the next chapter sits between the two: a cartoon, but one that shows steric shielding and more than one adsorbed species.

### What's in a name

The ZnS films were polycrystalline, so "epitaxy" was never strictly correct. As the materials list grew to amorphous oxides and nitrides, the name became a liability and was replaced by "atomic layer deposition". The same mismatch between name and physics applies to "atomic layer", since a cycle deposits a fraction of a monolayer (@sec-what-makes-ald).

## From displays to microchips

Finland stayed the centre of the field through the 1980s and 1990s:

- Lauri Niinistö started ALD process research at the Helsinki University of Technology in 1982. Espoo hosted the first ALE symposium in 1984 and the first international ALE symposium in 1990.
- Neste founded Microchemistry (Mikrokemia) in Espoo in 1987, with Suntola leading it, to apply ALD to catalysts and solar cells. Microchemistry also built some of the first commercial ALD reactors, the F120 series.
- Markku Leskelä and Mikko Ritala's group at the University of Helsinki developed much of the precursor chemistry, in a decades-long partnership with the reactor makers.

The turning point came in 1999, when ASM International (Netherlands) bought Microchemistry and refocused it on semiconductors. By then, the industry could see that the SiO~2~ gate dielectric would have to be replaced, and ALD could deposit the ultrathin high-k films needed. In 2007, Intel shipped 45 nm processors whose transistors used a hafnium-based high-k gate dielectric deposited by ALD, the first fundamental change to the CMOS transistor in four decades. ALD is now routine in logic, DRAM and 3D NAND manufacturing.

## A field with a conference and a name

The first AVS conference on ALD was held in Monterey, California, in 2001, chaired by Steven George; the second was held in Seoul in 2002 [@Parsons2013]. The annual meeting has since become the field's main venue, and since the mid-2010s it has been held jointly with the International Atomic Layer Etching Workshop. The 2024 meeting in Helsinki marked 50 years since the first ALE patent. Suntola received the Millennium Technology Prize for ALD in 2018.

## Recovering the history

Because the two lineages developed in isolation, the early literature is scattered across languages and journals. The **Virtual Project on the History of ALD** (VPHA) was started in July 2013 as an open, volunteer effort to make that early work visible [@Ahvenniemi2017]. Participants read and discussed early publications from both lineages. The result was a recommended reading list, presented at the ALD 2016 conference in Dublin and published the following year with dozens of co-authors [@Ahvenniemi2017].

//| echo: false
visible = places

    ? {type: "azimuthal-equidistant", rotate: [-v.center[0], -v.center[1]],

  return P.plot({
    width: w,
    height: v ? Math.round(w * 0.6) : Math.round(w * 0.5),

    color: {domain: lineages, range: lineageFill},
    r: {type: "identity"},
    marks: [
      P.sphere({fill: view === "Helsinki area" ? "#FFFFFF" : "#F7FBFF", stroke: "#8C8C8C"}),
      P.graticule({stroke: "#E3E3E3"}),
      view === "Helsinki area"

        : P.geo(v ? land50 : land110, {fill: "#EDEDED", stroke: "#8C8C8C", strokeWidth: 0.6}),
      // Labels only at the Helsinki scale; one mark per place so each can have its own offset.
      view === "Helsinki area"
        ? visible.map(d => P.text([d], {x: "lon", y: "lat", text: "label", dx: d.dx ?? 0, dy: d.dy ?? -16,
            textAnchor: d.anchor ?? "middle", fontSize: 13, stroke: "white", strokeWidth: 4, fill: "black"}))
        : null,
      P.dot(visible, {
        x: "lon", y: "lat", fill: "lineage", stroke: "#000", strokeWidth: 1.2,
        r: d => 6 + 1.5 * d.shown.length,
        channels: {Place: "name", Location: "where", Events: d => d.shown.length},
        tip: {format: {x: false, y: false, fill: false, r: false}}
      }),
    ]
  });
}

## Check your understanding

::: {.quiz}
Why did molecular layering remain largely unknown outside the USSR until the 2010s?

- [ ] It used chemistry that did not work outside a laboratory.
- [x] It was published mainly in Russian and developed with little contact with Western thin-film researchers.
- [ ] It was classified military research until 2013.
- [ ] It was a later copy of atomic layer epitaxy.

::: {.explanation}
Molecular layering predates ALE, so it was not a copy. The main barrier was language and isolation, which is exactly what the VPHA set out to address [@Ahvenniemi2017; @Malygin2015].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
What was the first industrial application of ALD?

- [ ] High-k gate dielectrics in microprocessors
- [ ] Copper diffusion barriers
- [x] ZnS-based thin-film electroluminescent displays
- [ ] Catalyst supports

::: {.explanation}
ALE was invented to make the thin, uniform, high-breakdown-strength films that EL displays need, and Lohja began producing displays in Espoo in the 1980s. Semiconductor use came about two decades later [@Puurunen2014].
:::
:::

::: {.quiz}
Why is "atomic layer epitaxy" a misleading name, even for Suntola's original ZnS films?

- [x] The films were polycrystalline, not epitaxial, and each cycle deposits less than one atomic layer.
- [ ] The films were grown from liquid precursors.
- [ ] ZnS cannot be grown epitaxially.
- [ ] The process was plasma-enhanced.

::: {.explanation}
"Epitaxy" means growth with a crystallographic relationship to the substrate, which the polycrystalline ZnS films did not have [@Puurunen2014]. "Atomic layer" overstates what one cycle deposits (@sec-what-makes-ald). Both terms record the technique's history rather than its physics.
:::
:::

## Further reading

- @Barry2022, Chapter 1: an introduction to ALD chemistry, including the history of both lineages.
- @Puurunen2014: the story of ALE as told by its inventor, written for the 40th anniversary. Open access.
- @Malygin2015: the first detailed English-language account of molecular layering and of Aleskovskii and Kol'tsov.
- @Ahvenniemi2017: the VPHA reading list of early publications from both lineages. Open access.
- @Parsons2013: how the ALD community and its conference grew within the AVS.
